transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-09-12 16:00 UTC | Duration 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Solutions), Aaron (Hearthline Head of AI), Lydia (Infra), Samir (PM), Noah (Procurement)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account.
[00:08] Aaron: Aaron here, head of AI at Hearthline. We're shipping personalized product recs and chat assistants. Latency matters, costs matter even more as this scales.
[00:18] Daniel: Cool, can you give a sense of traffic patterns and token counts? rough numbers are fine.
[00:24] Samir: Sure — peak is around 300 rps for the recommendation service, average prompt+completion is about 120 tokens, but we have lots of short hits (20-40 tokens) for micro-personalization. Monthly we expect ~150M tokens initially, aiming to 500M in six months.
[00:41] Priya: ok that's helpful, and SLO? latency targets?
[00:45] Aaron: 95th percentile under 220ms end-to-end for the quick path. For longer flows we can tolerate up to 500ms.
[00:54] Maya: Great. so the main theme today — we want to map economics: per-token pricing, how batching and caching reduce burn, and which hosting mode makes sense given your constraints. Also call out security and pilot next steps.
[01:08] Lydia: One caution — we have strict data residency and need SSO/SAML, SOC2, plus our key management uses Azure Key Vault/HSM. We can't do an unmanaged multi-tenant with logs leaving region without approval.
[01:22] Daniel: Understood. Redwood Hosted can do region controls and we have enterprise options for private plane — but we'll dig into that. first, pricing: for hosted, our list per-token is tiered — small customers see higher per-token, committed/Reserved (Dedicated) drops the effective unit price substantially.
[01:40] Samir: can you ballpark numbers? we need to feed procurement.
[01:44] Maya: Ballpark — hosted generation pricing for a mid-sized base model runs around $2.00 per 1k output tokens depending on model and sequence length; embeddings and smaller ops have different scales. With a dedicated reservation you'd see up to 40-60% reduction depending on committed tokens and model family. Also batching and kv/prefix caching can reduce effective tokens by 20-60% depending on reuse.
[02:03] Audience: (murmurs)
[02:07] Noah: So if we do 150M tokens a month, rough hosted cost would be...
[02:10] Maya: quick calc — 150M tokens is 150k * 1k tokens, sorry — uh, math — 150,000 * $2 = $300k a month ballpark for hosted generation tier. But that's before optimizations like caching, batching, quantized model families. With caching where repeated user prefixes hit cached KV entries you might cut that 30% easily, maybe more for repeat customers.
[02:36] Aaron: Those numbers are big. Our CFO will freak. What's the path to get that down to acceptable?
[02:42] Daniel: There are levers: 1) model choice/quantization — move to a smaller quantized variant for short responses; 2) batching — continuous batching on the runtime reduces per-request overhead and often reduces cost via GPU efficiency; 3) KV cache / prefix cache — for personalization many tokens can be served from cached KV; 4) routing policies — cheaper model variants for low-priority traffic or fallbacks.
[03:03] Samir: can batching increase latency? we can't add 200ms just to save $$
[03:07] Daniel: Good question — Redwood has latency-aware batching. for low-latency paths we keep micro-batches (1-8 requests) and set thresholds. Our runtime will prioritize latency SLO routes; you can set a max wait time (e.g., 10ms) so 95th stays low. For high QPS very short prompts, batching actually improves throughput and can lower average tail. There's a tradeoff but it's tunable.
[03:29] Lydia: And for private/on-prem? we need KMS integration and no logs leaving the VPC.
[03:33] Maya: Dedicated or Private gives you control. Private includes customer-managed control plane in your VPC, KMS integration — HSM is supported for encryption-at-rest keys — and audit logs stay within your tenant. Pricing is higher upfront (platform fee) but unit costs are lower once you amortize GPUs across steady throughput.
[03:51] Aaron: How long to spin up a dedicated cluster if we commit?
[03:54] Priya: Typical lead time is 2-6 weeks depending on capacity and region, can be accelerated for enterprise contracts. We also offer burst capacity from hosted as a fallback while the dedicated pool warms up.
[04:06] Samir: We think initial run will be a hybrid: hosted during playbook + pilot, then move to dedicated if numbers make sense. procurement wants cost certainty and SLA for 99.9 uptime for critical routes.
[04:17] Noah: Procurement question — on reserved nodes, how are overages billed and what about burst?
[04:21] Maya: Reserved capacity includes planned baseline. overage is billed at a discounted rate compared to on-demand hosted. Burst policies can be configured with caps to limit surprise charges. We'll include a modeled spreadsheet with examples.
[04:34] Aaron: Can you run a benchmark with our prompts? we want to see real token burn and latencies.
[04:38] Daniel: yes — if you upload an anonymized prompt set we'll run a 72-hour benchmark on hosted small-batch config and report: effective tokens, prefix cache hit rates, latencies, and model cost. That will show expected burn and recommended levers.
[04:53] Samir: what's the typical reduction from prefix caching for personalization workloads? we've seen wildly different numbers in past POCs.
[04:58] Daniel: It depends on the reuse pattern. For session-based personalization you might see 30-50% of tokens saved if user histories are reused; for global repeated prompts (like templated marketing) >60% possible. The benchmark will show us the hit rate on your real traffic pattern.
[05:15] Lydia: network-wise we need VPC peering — any surprises?
[05:18] Priya: We do egress peering and private endpoints for dedicated/private. there are standard network setup docs; often infra teams want a diagram which we'll provide. For hosted multi-tenant endpoints we provide region controls but not VPC peering — that's in private.
[05:33] Aaron: security checklist — SOC2, SAML/SSO, audit logs, KMS/HSM support?
[05:38] Maya: we are SOC2 Type 2. We support SAML SSO with SCIM provisioning, RBAC with token-scoped roles, audit logs (retention configurable on Enterprise), and KMS/HSM integrations for private cluster keys. we'll share the security whitepaper and compliance pack.
[05:53] Noah: Procurement will want example contract terms for data residency and liability caps.
[05:57] Maya: We'll include a sample enterprise addendum and SLA language in the proposal.
[06:03] Samir: Back to economics — if we target 300 rps peak, 120 tokens average and goal is $X per month — what's a realistic target for cost per 1k tokens when moving to dedicated?
[06:12] Daniel: If you commit to dedicated and tune caching/batching, many customers reach $0.30-$0.80 per 1k tokens on optimized pipelines depending on model family and quantization. For example, switching to a 4-bit quantized variant for short replies and aggressive caching, we often hit under $0.50 per 1k. But this is model- and workload-specific.
[06:32] Aaron: Ok so from $2 to ~0.5 with dedicated+ops — that's attractive. how much commit would push us into that range?
[06:38] Maya: commitments are based on reserved GPU hours or token commitments. Roughly, a 6-12 month commit that covers baseline peak capacity (your 300 rps sustained load) would push pricing to the lower range. We'll model a few scenarios in the spreadsheet: 3-month, 6-month, 12-month commits with usage tiers.
[06:55] Samir: are there hidden costs? like tokenization differences, system prompts eating tokens, or pre/post processing tokens?
[07:00] Daniel: yes — system prompts and few-shot examples count. pre/post tokens, and embedding calls also cost. We recommend measuring raw tokens at the request boundary and factoring in average of system messages. Some customers move static system content into server-side templates to reduce repetition. Also local cache of system responses can reduce calls.
[07:18] Lydia: What's the billing granularity — per-request or aggregated daily?
[07:22] Maya: We bill monthly with per-request metering aggregated by account and route. The console gives token-level breakdown per model and route so you can attribute spend to features.
[07:32] Aaron: Great, seeing the console visibility will help finance.
[07:36] Noah: For pilot scope, what do you suggest?
[07:39] Priya: Typical pilot: 6 weeks. Weeks 1-2 onboarding + telemetry + baseline on hosted. Weeks 3-4 run benchmarks and iterate on batching/caching/route config. Weeks 5-6 prove steady-state with cost model and pilot handoff plan to Dedicated if needed. We can compress to 4 weeks for urgent cases.
[07:58] Samir: can we start with a small sample of users? we prefer to limit exposure.
[08:02] Maya: yes — route-level segmentation and canary rollout is standard. We can pin pilot routes to hosted while other production traffic goes to your existing stack.
[08:11] Daniel: Also note — we offer intelligent routing so low-priority traffic can route to cheaper variants automatically; that can save cost without changing client logic.
[08:20] Aaron: Any caveats around model compatibility when falling back to cheaper variants — hallucinations, regressions?
[08:25] Daniel: That's why we run evals. We'll tie quality checks to prompt-level evals and can set automated fallback policies (A/B or similarity threshold) so you don't drop below quality floor. Redwood Optimize gives regression alerts.
[08:40] Priya: ok procurement note — we'll include clear run-rate and overage examples; also need termination clauses for private infra.
[08:47] Noah: yes please.
[08:50] Maya: Action items recap: we'll share pricing/spreadsheet, run benchmark given your prompts, schedule security deep-dive, and propose pilot timeline.
[08:58] Samir: fine. once we see numbers we'll decide on commit size.
[09:02] Aaron: anything else?
[09:04] Priya: one more question on observability — can we get token-level traces back to request IDs?
[09:09] Daniel: yes, the console supports per-request tracing, exports, and ingest hooks for your internal tracing. We can instrument to tag customer IDs to attribute cost.
[09:18] Aaron: ok good.
[09:20] Maya: I'll send the pricing + pilot proposal and security pack after the call. Daniel will run the bench. Aaron, if you upload the prompt set we'll start next week.
[09:29] Aaron: I'll do that today. thanks everyone.

(occasional crosstalk and brief pauses toward end)

End transcript.
